newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour asks how Major will fund pension reform.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour asks how Major will fund pension reform.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party on Wednesday attacked the Conservative government's plans for a "revolution" in Britain's pension system and asked where the money was going to come from to pay for it.
Labour's economics spokesman Gordon Brown accused Prime Minister John Major of wanting to privatise state pensions and putting at risk basic cover for people retiring in the future.

"The tax and spending problems with the Conservative pension proposals is utterly basic: there are huge front end costs which will run into billions of pounds and mean higher taxes for everyone," Brown told a news conference.

Brown said the cumulative public cost of the scheme would reach 151 billion sterling ($243.3 billion) by the year 2040 which would have to be funded through tax rises, even without setting aside money to guarantee basic pensions if private funds failed.
"How much will have to be set aside if private schemes fail? How much will people have to pay? Where is the money coming from?" Brown said.
The proposals announced by Major on Wednesday are aimed at preventing huge burdens falling on future taxpayers by making workers take responsibility for providing for their old age.

Britain has set aside more than its European partners for future pension liabilities. But economists still predict a pensions bombshell next century when a shrinking workforce will have to support growing numbers of retired people.

"This will put us another huge step ahead -- enabling us to sustain a healthy, low-tax economy for the future," said Major, unveiling complex proposals under which every individual would build up a personal fund to provide an income on retirement.
To feed the account, employees would be given a rebate on part of their national insurance conributions -- a payroll tax used to fund pensions and welfare benefits.
Major said the state would thus no longer have to finance basic pensions from tax revenues, saving the government around 40 billion pounds a year by the middle of next century.
Employees would choose which company they wanted to manage their money. But Major said the state would underwrite the scheme and guarantee that everyone received a basic pension.

Another aspect of the reforms, trailed in Wednesday's newspapers, would lead to the phasing-out of the state earnings-related pension scheme (SERPS), which provides about 6.5 million people with a second pension.
But Brown said this amounted to privatising the basic state pension without being able to guarantee that the new funds will cobver pension demands in the future.

Labour proposes retaining the basic state pension. It also proposes retaining SERPS as an option, while developing a new range of new second pensions for those who do not already have occupational pension schemes.
Labour's social security spokeswoamn, Harriet Harman, said Labour would study the proposals carefully, but questioned why Major had made the announcement so close to the election.
Major must call an election by May and polls put the Labour party far ahead, with a lead of around 18 points.
But Harman added: "We believe these policies present a chilling prospect for hard-working families and threaten growing insecurity in retirement." ($ = 0.620 British Pounds Sterling)
